input.candidate_statement: I would sort value-index pairs and use two pointers.

problem_context.title: Two Sum
problem_context.statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer target, return the indices of two distinct elements whose values add to target. You may return the two indices in either order.

items: Exactly one valid pair exists for every input used by this problem.

examples.explanation: The two equal values are separate array elements.

python.display_signature: def twoSum(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]

expected_approaches.summary: Store each seen value with its index and look up the complement before inserting the current item.
expected_approaches.applicability: An unsorted array with a unique target pair.
assumptions: Indices, rather than values alone, are required.
key_invariants: Before index i is inserted, the map contains only earlier indices.
A complement lookup therefore cannot reuse the current element.
tradeoffs: Uses auxiliary memory to avoid quadratic pair enumeration.
common_implementation_variants: insert then check while excluding the current index

alternative_approaches.summary: Enumerate every pair of distinct indices.
alternative_approaches.applicability: Small inputs or as a correctness baseline.
key_invariants: The inner index is always greater than the outer index.
tradeoffs: Simple but too slow for the largest inputs.
common_failure_modes: starting the inner loop at the same index

alternative_approaches.summary: Sort value-index pairs and move two pointers toward the target sum.
alternative_approaches.applicability: When retaining original indices alongside values is acceptable.
assumptions: Sorting must preserve each original index.
key_invariants: Increasing the left value raises the sum; decreasing the right value lowers it.
tradeoffs: Avoids hashing but requires index preservation.
common_failure_modes: returning sorted positions instead of original indices

reference_solutions.source_code: class Solution { public: vector<int> twoSum(vector<int> nums, int target) { unordered_map<int,int> seen; for (int i=0; i<(int)nums.size(); ++i) { int need=target-nums[i]; if (seen.count(need)) return {seen[need], i}; seen[nums[i]]=i; } return {}; } };

class Solution { public int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) { java.util.Map<Integer,Integer> seen=new java.util.HashMap<>(); for(int i=0;i<nums.length;i++){ int need=target-nums[i]; if(seen.containsKey(need)) return new int[]{seen.get(need),i}; seen.put(nums[i],i); } return new int[]{}; } }

invariants.diagnostic_goal: The complement map represents only values seen before the current index.

complexity_expectations.diagnostic_goal: Derive the expected linear scan rather than claiming a worst-case hash guarantee.

common_misconceptions.diagnostic_goal: Distinguish duplicate values from reusing one array element.
Distinguish expected hash lookup time from a universal guarantee.

failure_modes.diagnostic_goal: Avoid matching an item with itself when target is twice its value.

counterexamples.purpose: Exposes returning the same index for 3 + 3.
Requires preserving two distinct positions with the same value.

constraint_mutations.diagnostic_goal: Specify a deterministic result rule if more than one pair is allowed.

probe_opportunities.diagnostic_goal: Defend why checking before insertion prevents self-pairing.
Compare sorting plus two pointers with the complement map.

expected_good_signals: checks complement before inserting current value
sample_phrasings: What prevents this element from being paired with itself?

common_followups.diagnostic_goal: Clarify the expected-time assumption behind the complexity claim.
expected_good_signals: qualifies hash operations as expected or average case
weak_or_misconception_signals: claims hash lookup is always constant
sample_phrasings: Which operation makes this expected linear rather than a guaranteed bound?

common_followups.diagnostic_goal: Test whether original index provenance is retained.
sample_phrasings: What information must travel with a value when you sort?

level_considerations.guidance: Expect a defensible expected-linear complement-map solution.

interview_pack.reference_reasoning: The reviewed complement-map approach is a strong baseline, but plausible unlisted correct approaches remain valid and should be evaluated from their own reasoning.

technical_rationale_rubric.technical_issue: Explore the approach's cost and original-index consequence, not correctness confirmation.
